Morar Bhita: A massacre site still frozen in fear
2026-03-25T12:39:02+06:00 | Sushanta Ghosh
https://www.thedailystar.net/news/bangladesh/news/morar-bhita-massacre-site-still-frozen-fear-4135086

Fifty-five years after the Liberation War, residents of Baruipara in Harhar village, under Gournadi upazila of Barishal, still avoid a place known as Morar Bhita, which translates roughly to “house of the dead.”

The site lies hidden behind thick betel leaf gardens, swamps, and dense jungle. Locals say that not even daylight is enough to make it safe to enter.

On May 15, 1971, that fear was born. On that day, around 150 villagers who had sought refuge there were killed by the Pakistani army.

Since then, generations of men, women, children, and teenagers have grown up hearing the stories, speaking the name Morar Bhita in hushed tones, and avoiding the site altogether.

However, every December 14, local freedom fighters make their way into the overgrown area, carrying flowers and banners to pay tribute.

Avilash Nandi is believed to be the sole survivor from those caught in the direct line of fire at the site.

On that fateful May day in 1971, he was just three years old, hiding in a betel leaf garden with his mother, Nirmala Nandi, 55, and his sister, Anita, 7. During the firing, both his mother and sister were killed, and a bullet struck his leg.

Now 58, Avilash recounts what he later learned from relatives and villagers: he was rescued while lying on the chest of his dead mother, covered in blood. A bullet had pierced his leg, but a local doctor treated him well.

“In the absence of my mother, I grew up with my sisters,” Avilash shared. “But the pain of those days is still in my body. I do not generally go to the swamps and betel leaf garden where the firing took place.”

Most residents of the village were Hindu farmers who cultivated betel leaves. The area was surrounded by gardens and jungle, which many believed would provide safety when news spread of the army’s arrival.

But according to villagers, local collaborators guided the Pakistani army to the spot, after which they carried out an indiscriminate attack.

Freedom fighter Commander Kader Howlader said the army had set out from a camp at Ashwini Kumar School in Batajor.

“Hearing the news of the arrival of the Pakistan Army in the area, a section of the villagers hid in the betel leaf garden, jungle, and swamps. But even though they were hiding, the Pakistan Army, sensing it, opened fire on them,” the freedom fighter described.

According to him, 152 people, including women, men, and children, were shot dead that day.

This figure largely matches what locals claim: the population of the village at the time was around 400, and nearly one-third of the village was killed. The bodies were buried in a pit beside the betel garden.

Freedom fighter Ismat Hossain said that although some bodies were taken away by relatives, many remained.

“Even then, 92 bodies were buried there. Almost every family in Baruipara lost someone in the massacre.”

Eyewitnesses carry vivid memories.

Jagadish Chandra Mandal, one of them, said the killings were horrific, with victims ranging from a six-month-old baby to an 85-year-old man.

Another eyewitness, Dhiren Gain, was just 12 at the time. He recalled how he escaped.

“My brother Robin Gain, my uncle Dhiren Gain were hiding in this jungle. After receiving the news of the shooting, I drove into the canal and went to Chandrahar from here. Later, I got the news that my brother and uncle had been killed by the Pakistan Army.”

Five and a half decades later, the site remains unmarked. Villagers say they have long demanded a memorial to honour and preserve the memory of those killed, but their calls have gone unanswered.

Yet, fear lingers.

Tulsi Das, 62, summed it up simply: “We do not go to the place Morar Bhita due to fear and panic.”
